Compound interest is when the interest you earn on an investment starts earning its own interest. Think of it like a snowball rolling downhill: it starts small, but as it rolls, it picks up more snow, gets bigger, and rolls faster.

Here’s a simple example: If you invest $1,000 and it earns 10% interest in one year, you’ll have $1,100. The next year, you earn 10% on that $1,100, not just your original $1,000. So you get $110 in interest the second year, instead of $100. Over time, that extra growth adds up, and your money can grow much faster than with simple interest (which only pays on the original amount).

The key ingredients are time and a consistent rate of return. The longer your money compounds, the more dramatic the effect. That’s why starting early, even with small amounts, can make a big difference.

If you’re curious, a nearby historical experiment is to look at how a $10,000 investment in a broad U.S. stock index fund grew from 1980 to 2020—it’s a classic example of compounding over decades. Or, if you want to try it yourself, you could calculate how much a small monthly savings habit might grow over 10 or 20 years using a compound interest calculator.
